In-context segmentation transfers a target from an annotated reference image to a query image.
We compare two training-free systems, INSID3 and CG-ICS, to examine how visual correspondence and concept-guided search affect accuracy, reference sensitivity, and inference cost.
On COCO-$20^i$ and LVIS-$92^i$, CG-ICS achieves mean-fold class-pooled IoU of 72.17\% and 47.44\%, versus 57.65\% and 40.77\% for INSID3.
This improvement comes with 7.37--10.63 times greater mean inference latency on input pairs with the same runner GPU model and an additional language-model GPU.

Component experiments identify distinct sources of performance: INSID3 benefits from feature debiasing and region aggregation, whereas CG-ICS benefits strongly from combining a semantic concept with visual prompts.
Additional concept search yields only a 0.22-point equal-query IoU gain on COCO but a 2.30-point gain on LVIS.
In the paired-input cohort, visual prompting reduces the marginal gain from search.
Reference variation and small-target failures further distinguish the systems.
These findings motivate Agreement-Gated Search (AGS), for which we derive a cost--accuracy decomposition and specify a controlled evaluation.
The report combines completed comparative evidence with this extension, whose experimental results are pending.
Code is available at \url{https://github.com/AvianHan/CE6190-Visual-Understanding}.
In-context segmentation (ICS) identifies a target in a query image from a reference image and its binary mask.
This interface allows a user to specify the target visually, without annotating each query or fitting a new task-specific model.

Reliable transfer remains difficult: the same category can change appearance, the reference may emphasize only part of an object, and the query can contain visually or semantically similar distractors.
A practical system must resolve these ambiguities at an acceptable inference cost.
Recent foundation models support two distinct solutions.
INSID3 constructs a mask from frozen DINOv3 features through debiasing, clustering, and similarity aggregation~\cite{insid3,dinov3}.
CG-ICS generates language concepts from the reference, evaluates and searches these concepts, and combines them with visual prompts in SAM~3~\cite{cgics,sam3}.
Their central difference is how the reference becomes actionable evidence: direct visual correspondence in one system, and concept-guided segmentation supported by visual transfer in the other.
A headline accuracy comparison leaves important behavior unresolved.
An improvement may depend on the reference, arise from a particular processing stage, or require expensive search that benefits only some inputs.
Complete-system evaluation therefore needs to be connected to component interventions and measured cost.
This connection is also necessary for designing an efficient extension: search should be reduced where its marginal value is small, while preserving it where the initial prediction is inadequate.
We study these questions on COCO-$20^i$ and LVIS-$92^i$ using common reference/query inputs and original-resolution evaluation.
CG-ICS is more accurate overall, while INSID3 is substantially faster.
The component results sharpen this comparison: a single concept combined with visual prompts captures most of CG-ICS's gain on COCO, whereas LVIS benefits more from further search.
Moreover, visual prompting reduces the marginal search gain on both datasets.
This measured interaction motivates an input-dependent search rule based on agreement between text-only and visual-only predictions.
Our contributions are threefold:
\textbf{Paired system evaluation.} We compare accuracy, reference sensitivity, and computational cost on common inputs.
\textbf{Component analysis.} We separate feature processing, semantic search, visual prompting, and backbone choice through controlled interventions.
\textbf{Agreement-Gated Search.} We propose input-dependent search with an explicit cost--accuracy formulation and predefined controls.
The empirical conclusions use the completed first batch; the extension is being evaluated separately on fresh queries and transfer datasets.
